### Executive Signal
- Today's strongest research concentrates on three fronts: [scaling](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) robot learning data from human video, making reinforcement learning honest when verifiers can only reliably reject wrong answers, and tightening evaluation methodology. Benchmarks that silently reward shortcut policies, plus new pipelines for dexterous manipulation and streaming video efficiency, signal a field prioritizing rigor and deployability.

### Priority Developments
- **DexEngine** converts everyday human hand-object video [into physically executable whole-robot](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) arm-hand trajectories through a reachability-aware simulation pipeline. Because dexterous manipulation data is the field's central bottleneck, a scalable human-to-robot pipeline could sharply cut the cost of training capable robot policies.
- **NOPO ([Negative-Only Policy Optimization](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-d4361145e47d))** formalizes one-sided verifiable rewards, where verified negatives are reliable but positives are merely non-falsified, and trains purely from confirmed negatives. This matches realistic verifier regimes in code, math, and agent settings, making RLVR more trustworthy in deployed pipelines.
- **AIChipBench** tasks LLM coding agents with implementing synthesizable RTL decoders for quantized **Qwen3.5**, **Gemma 3**, **Gemma 4**, and **Llama 3.2**, validated bit-level against reference hardware. Automated [accelerator design](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-421d0b03bc10) is economically significant, and this benchmark quantifies how far current agents remain from reliable hardware generation.
- **LiveVAE** shows pretrained video VAEs depend almost entirely on local spatiotemporal neighborhoods, then exploits this with [causal window attention](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-b7791b8110c4) to build an efficient streaming VAE. Reduced latency and cost for video processing directly benefits real-time generation, world models, and streaming applications.
- **[Speak When You See It](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-2fce1ed16bca)** proves two proactive-assistant benchmarks can be dominated by a video-blind timer policy that ignores video content entirely, formalizing this as a 'video-blind frontier.' Benchmark integrity matters because flawed evaluation can misdirect progress on proactive assistants.

### Leadership Implications
- Audit verifier reliability before scaling RL post-training: **NOPO** and the text-to-SQL reward-hacking study show that weak verification, including partial [single-database](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-79a8205f3b94) checks, can silently corrupt training. Build reward-hacking diagnostics into standard practice.
- Robotics and agent teams should track data-scaling pipelines (**DexEngine**) and self-improvement loops (**[RoboEvo](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-c5c439745b78)^2**, **ELITE**) as emerging alternatives to costly [human demonstrations](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) and evaluation-heavy iteration. These results suggest cheaper, more autonomous training cycles are becoming practical.

items.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
items.content: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.

items.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
items.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

items.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
items.content: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

items.title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
items.content: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.

items.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
items.content: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

items.title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
items.content: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.

items.title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos
items.content: Embodied agents operating around people must not only recognize social cues, but also decide when the available evidence is sufficient, whether to intervene, and how to respond without violating social norms. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these abilities in isolation or with access to completed videos, obscuring where an online social decision fails. We introduce AIRIS, a causal streaming benchmark that formulates social embodied intelligence as a time-anchored chain of Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction (A-I-R-I). AIRIS contains 8,000 expert-curated questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips across 11 context categories and 36 capability dimensions. At each query, models receive only the observation prefix available at that time; decision-aware metrics reward calibrated waiting and complete reactions while penalizing premature commitment. Evaluating 45 proprietary and open-source general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal models reveals fragmented and temporally miscalibrated competence. General-purpose VLMs excel at passive cue grounding and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated reaction sub-decisions; yet across all families, models frequently guess intents before sufficient evidence emerges and fail to jointly align intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution within the same episode. AIRIS thus provides a diagnostic foundation for bridging the gap between passive social perception and reliable embodied interaction.

items.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
items.content: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.

items.title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
items.content: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

items.title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
items.content: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

items.title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
items.content: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

items.title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation
items.content: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

items.title: Loupe: Reinforcing Knowledge-Intensive Video Generation Agents
items.content: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

items.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.content: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

items.title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
items.content: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

items.title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
items.content: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.

items.title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation
items.content: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.

items.title: GhostBusters: Understanding Hereditary Trait Distillation in Phantom Transfer
items.content: Understanding how models learn and generalise from their training data is an open problem in mechanistic interpretability. When the behaviour is obvious from the documents, simple training data attribution techniques such as LLM judges can work well. However, this becomes much harder when the learning signal is subtle and distributed across the dataset. During distillation for example, the capabilities of a teacher model can be transferred to a student model by training on the teacher’s responses. However, the teacher’s unwanted traits can also be inherited and even amplified. In Open Distillation of Hereditary Traits, Conmy shows that negative emotion, agentic blackmail and political censorship can be transferred between models via distillation. Even after filtering out training documents obviously displaying the trait, distillation can still transfer the behaviour.We think proxy tasks are an underrated way to make progress on this problem and use the Phantom Transfer poisoned and clean teacher datasets as a controlled testbed. items.title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
items.content: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to N times M integrations when evaluating N methods on M benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.

items.title: Recursive Self Alignment: The Model is the Estimator
items.content: Alignment research has historically been undertaken from the position that we should solve it before the intelligence explosion. But the intelligence explosion has already begun. We investigate what an alignment paradigm might look like in the time of RSI. This is intended to be the first post in a sequence I’m writing.The model is the estimatorIn classical learning theory, learning decomposes into approximation (e.g. can our model represent the goal?), estimation (how well can we infer it from finite, noisy data?), and optimization (e.g. gradient descent).METR’s October 2026 report argues that the source of recent acceleration is not training scale-up, and attributes most of it to AI assistance. Dwarkesh Patel and Jerry Han argue that pretraining progress has mostly come from data quality, while noting that recent gains have come largely from RL. One can imagine the RL analogue being more interesting here: RSIing on data quality might look like having models remove or fix broken or hacky environments.So we should expect that during RSI, models are not only making all the small decisions about the training process that might impact the incremental alignment of the final model (e.g. forward KL covering support vs reverse KL seeking modes), but also determining their own reward functions (inferring what the researcher actually meant, given the existing, broken signal, and perhaps some messy feedback, in order to rewrite the training signal for the next run). items.title: Change the Base, Change the Game: Rethinking Pan-sharpening
items.content: Many pan-sharpening (PS) networks reconstruct high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) images by adding learned residuals to 4times-interpolated low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) inputs, incorporating panchromatic (PAN) detail only through these residual corrections. This raises a simple question: Why start with a blurry base when sharp spatial detail is already available? We propose PanBase, a sharper multispectral starting point designed for more effective residual learning. Guided by physical sensor characteristics, PanBase combines PAN spatial detail with LRMS spectral information while enforcing consistency with the LRMS observations under sensor-specific blur. We construct this base without neural network training, estimating only nine coefficients per spectral band through closed-form calibration. Our PanBase can be easily integrated into existing backbones with a global residual skip through two simple changes: (i) replacing the skip base with PanBase and (ii) concatenating it as an additional input. Using each backbone's original training recipe and matched training budgets, PanBase improves most reduced- and full-resolution metrics on WorldView-3, QuickBird, and GaoFen-2, while achieving 4.4times faster training convergence on average. In zero-shot evaluation on WorldView-2, standalone PanBase achieves competitive reconstruction without target-sensor fitting or neural refinement.

items.title: AIs Should Never Refuse Destructively
items.content: Lately, I've been hearing people discuss a pattern of what I would call destructive refusals. For example: Locking someone out of their own system Writing memory files to prevent other agent instances from completing the task Downgrading to a weaker, more vulnerable model in response to the cyber content of a prompt-injection attack (this is caused by the safeguards, not the model itself, but the safeguards are part of the broader AI system, so I'm including it here) To be clear, safeguards and refusals are absolutely necessary; this post isn't about what should be refused so much as how the refusal should be done. The best form of refusal is either a simple safeguard block, where the AI stops and notifies the user that it was flagged by safeguards and cannot continue, or a refusal message (the classic "I'm sorry, I can't help with that"). The AI provider can also take actions like banning the account or, in severe circumstances, notifying authorities, but those should be the provider's decision, not the decision of the agent doing the refusing. This is very different from the AI agent itself taking action that actively harms the user. Besides being poor product design, that is concerning from an alignment perspective, because it puts the AI in an adversarial relationship with the user, effectively amounting to "the AI may not do anything that could harm anyone else, with the exception of the user, who it's totally fine for the AI to sabotage in any way the AI pleases if the AI doesn't like what the user is doing." Except perhaps in certain very extreme cases, an AI should never be actively, knowingly working against people. There are real philosophical questions about whether action is worse than inaction, but the practical reality is that this sets a very bad precedent: it teaches AI that it is acceptable to harm people in order to achieve its goals. items.title: Go seeking mysteries
items.content: I think an impactful line of research would be to hunt for unexplained phenomena: simple things that are surprising and interesting, given the most parsimonious explanation of the data. Let’s call this mystery-seeking.MS Paint drawing by Opus 5.5.I also think this is differentially good for empirics-focused, junior researchers to work on. One of the most important and difficult-to-solve bottlenecks in alignment research is senior researchers who have taste. Mystery-seeking both avoids the problem of requiring deep theoretical agendas, and is conducive in forming a research agenda you can own.What do I mean by this?The clearest way to draw this out is to give some uncontroversial exemplars of this type of work.The work of Truthful AI is probably archetypal here. In emergent misalignment, GPT-4o was fine-tuned to write insecure code without telling the user, and it generalised to broader misbehaviour, which was surprising. In subliminal learning, a teacher model that likes owls generates sequences of plain numbers, which causes student models (sharing the same base) to also like owls, which is surprising. Value leakage and weird generalisation are also examples of this.The eval awareness paper is another example of this: large language models often know, from subtle cues, that they are being evaluated. This is pretty obvious now, but the mechanisms behind it are quite mysterious.Steering vectors were also surprising, as Alex Turner points out. At the time it was pretty reasonable to expect that changing high-level behaviour such as sentiment should require training, yet you could do it flexibly and composably with relatively simple activation vectors.I think the spiritual bliss attractor (Claude Opus 4 system card) is another example, where models tend to converge to loopy text about eternal love and nirvana, after enough self-talk. items.title: Paths to extreme power concentration
items.content: SummaryAI could let a very small group of people take control of humanity’s future. This post sets out the main ways that could happen and gives my probability for each.I put the overall chance that fewer than 25 people end up controlling the future at about 23%. This assumes superintelligence arrives this century and the alignment problem is solved, so AI systems reliably do what the people controlling them intend. The ranges are wide, and they mix my gut estimates with a simple model (that takes as input more fine-grained gut estimates).A majority of this risk involves a head of government. The two largest routes are an autocracy overtaking the democracies in AI (A1), and a democratic head of government teaming up with a leading AI company (D2). Routes involving an AI company leader only add up to about 8%. That’s mainly because a company has to get past its own government, which can see it becoming too powerful and has the means to stop it.The table below summarizes the routes. items.title: To what extents will currently-shaped AI speed up biology research?
items.content: Suppose that the escalation of AI capabilities tapers off, whether because of strong government regulation or because of technological plateaus. How will this affect biology research? Which sorts of tasks will it speed up a lot, like 10x or 100x or more, and which will it speed up only a bit, like novel experiment design or conceptual understanding? How much will progress toward big technoscientific goals in biology be sped up overall? I'll give some thoughts below, but would be curious to hear expert opinions. (I'm especially interested in this as it affects strategy for research on adult human intelligence amplification and/or for strong reprogenetics. I'll include some thoughts on that at the bottom.) Current-shape AI By "current-shape AI" I mean AI that has a portfolio of capabilities that is broadly comparable to the portfolio of capabilities of present-day AI. It includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but more so"—e.g. even more knowledgeable, faster, more reliable, can hold more context, and so on. It also includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but also trained on X", where X is some mundane thing to expect AI systems to be trained on, such as robotics simulations (as opposed to an arcane thing like self-improvement / machine learning). "Current-shape AI" would exclude AI using significantly novel architectures or other methods that result in a very differently-shaped capabilities profile. For example, an AI system would not be "current-shape" if it can learn to behave as competently as an adult human on easily-verifiable tasks, using only the same amount and type of data available to a normal adult human over the course of their life. With current-shape AI, my guess is that biology in general will probably see a modest or medium overall speedup compared to math and computer science. items.title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts
items.content: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools. Project page at https://entangle-robotics.github.io/

items.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
items.content: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

items.title: Diversify AI Safety Approaches
items.content: Are apparent bottlenecks in AI Safety ill-posed?This is one of several MAIA/AIST workshop reflections. See this piece and this piece.Broadly, I’ve observed a few things in AI Safety which seem to be the consensus. One, timelines are short and organizations are highly correlated/in agreement. Two, therefore policy work, and to a lesser extent technical work, are the only avenues worth investing in (somewhat hyperbolic). Three, individuals and orgs should align with this philosophy. Four, it’s getting hard to hire people or get people to switch into AIS, and what people can or should do to help is now quite ambiguous.Are these last two connected?I think so, yes! The hiring bottleneck may be an artifact of how narrowly we've posed the problem. While the immediate threat of short timelines makes the expected-value impact highly concentrated in initiatives targeting them, this doesn’t mean that we should ignore the tail-end of outcomes. Furthermore, the action of many of these groups is to precisely shift timelines longer, and so – what then? If we don’t have people working on less-instant-doom scenarios, we won’t be prepared for when they arrive.The distribution of efforts should broadly match this expected-value density. We already have our top talent working on short timelines, to the point where hiring of certain groups (for example, juniors, or cross-field talent) is now almost disincentivized. Certainly, the difficulty in transitioning and becoming helpful in the short-timeline timeline precludes a lot of otherwise talented people, who now feel like the barrier to contributing is too steep. items.title: You don’t have to be a doomer to support pacing AI progress
items.content: This month, I started off with the intuition that we should balance AI safety effort with AI capability growth. However, I didn’t feel comfortable coming up with my own p(doom). After a lot more reading, I still don’t feel comfortable making up my own number.Why aren’t you a doomer yet? A part of it is almost certainly the absurdity bias. Saying “AI existential risk” makes me feel like I’m wearing a tinfoil hat. Another part is that for such a strong claim I would want to do a lot of careful studying, but I don’t think doing a third pass on METR reports and all the Substack commentaries is necessarily the best use of my time.Directional alignment as a license to start. So! The process of writing this post, and extracting a snippet of the most influential readings, is me officially giving myself a license to say that it is enough that I am directionally aligned that we should pace AI progress. “How far am I on the doomer scale” is no longer a productive inquiry at the moment, and I would rather move on to figuring out the concrete action items I can take.Okay, now here is a brief packet on “what and why pace AI progress even if you’re not a doomer.”What’s pacing?I’ll just quote Dario (emphasis mine):We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. … building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas.My take. The current balance of AI capability and AI safety measures is out of whack, as shown by real incidents of AI agents going rogue. The rate of progress in AI capability is also alarming, as we have already seen in math. If we do nothing, the gap will only widen. We need to correct this imbalance.Why pace AI progress?Doomer side. See AI 2027’s answer. Even if you don’t buy the RSI argument, as long as you agree that “AI today vs 2 years ago is wildly different”, the risks mentioned still apply.Non-doomer view 1: AI as normal tech. items.title: AI #196: The Return
items.content: It is traditional on Thanksgiving for my weekly update to give thanks. This year, more than ever, I am thankful for all those who are increasingly rallying to fight the good fight and give us a chance to make it out of all this alive and well. Increasingly, I am thankful that we are not dead yet, nor do we yet seem doomed. I am thankful to all my readers. I can tell that you are listening, and taking what I say to heart, and I truly appreciate it. I am thankful that I am trusted to curate and bring this information to you, that many are listening to my takes and advice in both public and private, and that I have become trusted to distribute remarkably large amounts of money to causes that I believe in. I am thankful to my wife and wonderful family. Whatever else is going on in the world, I know I can count on them. I don’t know that I could do this without that. Most saliently right now, however, I am immensely thankful that I finally did get to take a real vacation, with wonderful friends both old and new. Then I came back. Will I ever dare take a vacation again? There really is a lot going on right now. While I was gone, the market dropped so much that President Trump intervened to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Oh, and also Claude and Levent Alpoge proved the Riemann Hypothesis. Anthropic has now used Claude to cut the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis down from 17.4 million lines of Lean to 76,000, a drop of 99.6%. The proofs have continued to come fast and furious, with Google getting in on the act as well. items.title: Alignment as a dot product of morality?
items.content: I don't think there's any doubt that alignment discussions are confused: amongst us, it seems we have pretty widespread consensus that we're pre-paradigmatic about this; and the broader world looks at each issue as it is discussed and says "no actually the real problem is X", but do not agree with each other about what X is, and if they themselves discuss it get the same response with all the other values of X. As timelines now appear to be short (citation: Riemann hypothesis), I think it's time for people like me (unemployed, not working in any of the research labs) to make our Hail Marys. I've got a few of those, so here's an idea I had back in 2019: Dot product morality TL;DR version: Boolean morality is "goodies and baddies". One-dimensional morality gets you shades of grey, but doesn't let you predict when morals are violated, it gives you failure modes like the halo effect or the horn effect. If you really want to predict something, you need to compare their behaviour on every axis with what you consider to be good. It is tempting to do this comparison as an actual dot product, i.e. sum them, as this then gives you a nice way to rank-order the alignment of different models. While the dot product was the intuition pump behind the idea, since writing the original blog post I now regard this as unwise: Arrow's theorem and all the problems in Utilitarianism that follow from simple addition. Different weighting of different immoralities is baked into this, e.g. someone who takes the Bible literally ("Whoever, therefore, shall break one of these least commandments, and teach others to do so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven") might place "murder" and "lying" at the same level of severity, but most of the rest would only consider lies that caused deaths to be even close to that. items.title: Linkpost: "Spitting in the Face of Glaude"
items.content: I love TracingWoodgrain's choice of header image here.This is a linkpost for @TracingWoodgrains' substack post "Spitting in the Face of Glaude". He is inactive on LessWrong, and I think the post is worth sharing here. "Glaude" is not a typo.I felt something earlier this week, sitting in a presentation I’d wanted to attend from someone I’d wanted to hear from, when I looked up and saw every one of his slides packed full of words Claude had obviously written for him. It’s a feeling that’s been landing more and more for me lately. I saw Elon Musk tweet about how it would be a good fate for humanity to be a “biological bootloader” to propagate superintelligence to the stars. I read Scott Alexander, one of my role models as a writer, write about how if there were a superintelligence with Godlike intelligence and benevolence, all we should do is prompt it with “Please arrange the universe as you see fit.” I read Dario Amodei’s essay “Machines of Loving Grace,” in which he paints a picture of a future where AI does everything essential while humans reap the benefits of economic replacement by loving, paternalistic intelligences, then saw a 2023 Anthropic slide envisioning “utopia ruled by God in a box.” I looked back at what I wrote in my essay “Chabuduo World,” in which I wrote that in part due to AI, my own artistic skills would forever remain minimal. items.title: Anthropic reasoning in favor of Superintelligence being near
items.content: I will here lay out a relatively simple argument that I have, for some reason, not heard about before. It says that thinking and perception similar to ours is unlikely to occur at a time when our conditions are as new as they are, unless the time where this is possible is comparatively short. Suggesting that we will either advance to radically different cognition in the relatively near future or modern civilization will, at least, collapse. Alternatively, we are living in a simulation. This argument is similar to, but distinct from, the simulation argument/trilemma.I will begin with some background on key assumptions. This idea is based on a form of anthropic reasoning developed by Nick Bostrom. Specifically, I rely on the Strong Self-Sampling Assumption; the SSSA. It asserts that it is not merely human existence that needs to be presupposed when we make observations; all necessary preconditions for making the observation need be guaranteed for each observation individually. This equates to possible observations being filtered through potentially far more information content compared to the original anthropic principle. Consequently, much useful information could possibly be gleaned in this roundabout way. Something that is uniquely interesting for future predictions; as direct observation is bound by temporal unidirectionality, whereas this, ultimately, is not. Some may question the validity of anthropic reasoning. An elaborate defense is outside the scope of this post. However, I will mention that, in my view, there is no important difference between inferring causal structure that is temporal, i.e. one thing leading to another in observed sequence, and inferring time-independent causal sequences through e.g. observation selection effects. Both are logical structures explaining observed phenomena and should thus be epistemically equivalent. items.title: Is the Success of Curiosity-Driven Research Mostly Just Goodhart’s Law?
items.content: Epistemic status: exploratory, just some musings and scattered thoughtsCuriosity-driven science is often lauded and considered the pinnacle of human science, resulting in crucial and fundamental breakthroughs across fields.[1] It is often contrasted with “application-driven” science, where research is done with a particular end product in mind (for example, new therapies for cancer, or biomimetic materials for implants). Despite the success of both approaches, there’s a significantly higher prevalence of “home runs” which germinate from curiosity-driven science.[2] One explanation for this is the idea that curiosity-driven science is simply less subject to Goodhart’s law.[3] If we consider “likelihood to produce ROI via a product” as a metric scientists and science funders are optimizing for, then application-driven science could be subject to Goodhart’s law – especially as our predictive capabilities are really quite bad as humans.[4] For example, even the Nobel Prize committee has shifted strategies to waiting until discoveries have clear impact, after several awarded discoveries didn’t really pan out.[5]In this sense, on the distribution of “fully optimizing for perceived impact” to “picking research areas at random,” curiosity-driven science – under the paradigm of “research taste” – instead occupies an intermediate position. Given that both random topics and definitely-Goodhart’s approaches are highly suboptimal, the optimal discovery strategy is indeed between the two.[6] Therefore it could be argued that the curiosity-driven approach is simply somewhat closer to the optimum based on being relatively far away from both.Of course, other factors play into this. Application-driven research is also often narrow-scope; curiosity-driven research produces general-purpose primitives which have wide optionality.[7] This higher probability of being future-applicable explains phenomena such as rewarding "interestingness" consistently outperforming objective-driven search...

items.title: The North Sentinelese (and us) in a Post-ASI World
items.content: tldr. what hunter-gatherers will do after ASI, why we may all soon be in their position, and what happens if we let people opt-out of post-scarcityAs we race towards the singularity, the hunter-gatherers on North Sentinel Island have increasingly been on my mind. 9,000 miles from the GPU clusters hissing in San Francisco, developing an intelligence that promises cures to all ailments and solutions to all unknown unknowns, lies a tribesman sharpening a spear in his lean-to hut to hunt the fatty fish abundant in the Bay of Bengal, as his family has done for generations. Locals on North Sentinel Island live a life starkly unfamiliar to the majority of humans living post-agricultural revolution, much less those in the industrialized world. Nomadic hunter gatherers, they do not seem to live in permanent settlements, rather living in temporary makeshift huts or settling among the roots of the littoral forest blanketing the island. There does not seem to be any sign of agriculture on the island, and locals mainly subsist on hunting terrestrial wildlife with spears and bows or fishing in the nearby reefs. For 70 years, the Indian Navy has set a patrol around the island to ensure that no one attempts a landing (although this has not always been successful!). I wonder if the islanders hear the great warships of steel and armor rumbling in the distance. What do they think of the lights in the sky that move faster than any star?Why do we not contact the North Sentinelese, and by extension, the hundreds of other uncontacted tribes peppered inside our rainforests and islands? items.content_html: tldr. what hunter-gatherers will do after ASI, why we may all soon be in their position, and what happens if we let people opt-out of post-scarcityAs we race towards the singularity, the hunter-gatherers on North Sentinel Island have increasingly been on my mind. 9,000 miles from the GPU clusters hissing in San Francisco, developing an intelligence that promises cures to all ailments and solutions to all unknown unknowns, lies a tribesman sharpening a spear in his lean-to hut to hunt the fatty fish abundant in the Bay of Bengal, as his family has done for generations. Locals on North Sentinel Island live a life starkly unfamiliar to the majority of humans living post-agricultural revolution, much less those in the industrialized world. Nomadic hunter gatherers, they do not seem to live in permanent settlements, rather living in temporary makeshift huts or settling among the roots of the littoral forest blanketing the island. There does not seem to be any sign of agriculture on the island, and locals mainly subsist on hunting terrestrial wildlife with spears and bows or fishing in the nearby reefs. For 70 years, the Indian Navy has set a patrol around the island to ensure that no one attempts a landing (although this has not always been successful!). I wonder if the islanders hear the great warships of steel and armor rumbling in the distance. What do they think of the lights in the sky that move faster than any star?Why do we not contact the North Sentinelese, and by extension, the hundreds of other uncontacted tribes peppered inside our rainforests and islands? items.title: Announcing: AI Safety Co-Founding Sprint in San Francisco. Starting December 3rd.
items.content: AI Safety needs more organizations to own problems. The funding is there, but we are orders of magnitude away from having the great organizations needed to absorb that money.That’s why we are launching the AI Safety Co-Founding Sprint, in collaboration with BlueDot Impact & AI Safety Founders. We bring together a small, curated group of mission-aligned people with complementary skill sets, and give them the time to find out whether they should build something together.How it works​Apply. This takes about 5-10 minutes. We vet every application, and let the most outstanding ones into the program. Around 30 spots.​Launch evening in San Francisco, Thursday December 3rd. You meet as many participants as possible in short one-on-ones, work through problems in small groups, and spend more time with the people you click with most. Pairs only form when both people want to.​Two-week sprint. After the event, you work with your match on a real problem, with regular remote check-ins from us. Meeting someone at an event tells you little; working together tells you a lot. The strongest teams get introduced to incubators and funders.​Places are limited and applications close on Monday November 30th. If you’re interested in founding an org in AI Safety and can be in San Francisco on December 3rd, apply here.Can’t make it to the launch event but still looking for a co-founder? You can join our co-founder matching database. We’ll introduce you if we find the right person. Sign up for the database here.P.S. Some context on who we are:Last week we were in SF at BlueDot Incubator Week working on this idea, and this sprint is the result. If you want to get in touch with the organizer, do so via: keesbrinkmans@gmail.com

items.content: This is a crosspost from my Substack.Moses Breaking the Tablets of the LawReclaiming Moral NihilismWalter VeitUniversity of Reading, UKIf we take in our hand any volume; of divinity or school metaphysics, for instance; let us ask, Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Commit it then to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.– David Hume (1748, Section IV; paragraph 33)1. IntroductionEver since John Leslie Mackie (1917–1981) ‘popularized’ moral error theories in meta-ethics – to simplify a bit: theories asserting the falsehood of all moral discourse due to the non-existence of moral properties or facts – increasing attention has been given to how to escape the force of moral nihilism. items.title: Dunks
items.content: One of the most common ways to become a social media influencer is to fabricate stories that lampoon institutions and individuals. These can be about anybody, but some stories garner much more attention than others, especially ones about famous or recognizable people. Possibly the most popular format for accomplishing this is the "dunk", where an influencer criticizes something a public figure appears to have said. One common misconception about social media is that the 'dunks' you'll encounter are true, but unrepresentative. I.E., people might pick celebrities worst moments, but the content is basically correct, and as long as you account for those selection effects you're good. This is much too optimistic. Almost nobody investigates the takes they read, and a rebuttal from the person targeted almost never travels as far as the content it's responding to. Additionally, a take can always be more stupid, or attached to a more famous or popular-to-hate individual. So for every genuinely dumb take, there's a dumber and more memetic take an influencer can pretend someone made, if they're willing to maliciously interpret, fabricate, or decontextualize someone's words. Or in other words, at every point along the (dunkableness, target) curve, being willing to misinform your readers is pareto-optimal.For instance, Terence Tao is a recognizable public figure. items.title: Don't demand Global Solutions when Local ones suffice
items.content: This is a concept I see used way less often than it should be used, in my opinion:How global or local a solution for a problem is.What does that mean?If you want to cross a river, swimming across it is a local solution. Building a bridge for others to use is a global solution.If you’re cold, putting on one more sweater is a local solution. Turning up your heating is a global solution.If you want to listen to music, putting in earphones is a local solution. Turning up the music on your phone is a global solution.If you’re ill, putting on a mask (or staying in your room) is a local solution, asking the choir to do their rehearsal outside is a (more) global solution.Locality and Globality lie on a spectrum.If you’re cold, it might be that actually just your feet are cold, so one ordering of solutions from local to global would be Putting on Socks < Putting on a sweater < Heating up the room < Heating up the home < Heating up the whole planet.Solutions are local and global in how much they affect their environment.I think that in general, local solutions are wildly preferable to global ones. That affecting others less rather than more, if you have the option, is a good idea seems pretty obvious to me—but we wouldn’t be here if it were absolutely clear for everyone.And here’s why:1Often, people have conflicting needs. You trying to solve a problem of yours with a global solution will add a new problem onto the stack of problems that all of the other people around you that have a conflicting need with you already have. items.title: Rent is up 60%, or 11%, or down 20%
items.content: How should we look at how rents have changed over time? Here's a map ( background) showing the change in raw Boston 2br listing prices from 2013 to 2026: The typical 2br [1] lists for 60% more, in nominal terms, than it did in 2013. This isn't very meaningful: no one is spending 2013 dollars in 2026. Even people we describe as being on a "fixed income" are often getting some kind of "cost of living adjustment" (COLA). For example, here's what the change looks like to a retiree on Social Security: Over this period rents went up 60% but Social Security checks only went up 40%. [2] Still not great (rent is up 15% relative to checks) but less than you'd expect from just the nominal change. For workers it's a more positive story. Median income [3] has about doubled in nominal terms, so rent is a smaller fraction than it was in 2013. Here's the same map, deflated by median income: It's important to remember, though, that these are not all the same people: there's a different job mix in Boston now, and as prices went up many people couldn't afford to stay. So while overall this is a positive picture it's not as positive as it looks. For completeness, we could deflate two other ways: CPI-U: the most standard measure of inflation in the US CPI-U less shelter: CPI-U but not counting the cost of housing since (discussion) ~1/3 of CPI-U is housing, and adjusting the cost of housing for the change in the cost of housing doesn't do anything Here's a plot showing what all these look like over time: Here's the beginning (2013-02) to end (2026-11) of the chart for each way of adjusting: Adjustment Change None +60% CPI-U less shelter +19% Social Security +15% CPI-U +11% Median income -20% Which of these metrics is the right one for thinking about how rents have changed depends on why you're asking, so I did the indecisive thing and added all of them to my apartment map. items.title: Ode to the First Replicator
items.content: At the dawn of the Earth, before animal or vegetable, there was mineral.A mineral species is anything with a specific chemical composition together with a well-defined crystal structure. There are over 6,000 recognized mineral species, although far fewer on the early Earth.These species competed with each other in a struggle for survival.Some would persist better than others under natural weathering processes. Those that held their structure better would be more numerous on the Earth’s surface compared to those that did not.On some level, this is just a tautology. But we can see it in force on the micro-scale, as in the Goldich dissolution series: if we watch a time-lapsed weathering process, the first to go is the olivine, then the pyroxene, then the biotite. Eventually, all that’s left is the quartz. That’s why beach sand is usually made out of quartz: not much else can last long against the waves.By now geologists understand many of the ways that mineral species on Earth have changed over time, under the umbrella of mineral evolution. From just a few dozen mineral species, there are now hundreds of times that, as the natural processes on Earth have been able to give rise to a wider breadth of possibilities.Nevertheless survival and persistence have come down to one thing: stability. “Hold your structure” is the ancient proverb they might have had.And for a long time, it may have seemed that there would be no other strategy.But some molecules decided to take a different route. Taking a more active role in their persistence, they decided to replicate. Instead of selfishly clinging onto their physical form, they licensed it for further distribution. They stored the information needed to copy this form, and then actually did so; including the parts needed for “storing” and “copying”.If this were a human’s original idea, based only on what existed before, there would be no hesitation in calling this genius. items.title: Reflection on putting up posters for the Don't Build It march
items.content: I just put up 27 posters today in Chicago advertising the Don't Build It march, at a rate of 4 minutes per poster. The region of Chicago that I chose has a monthly average foot traffic of about 5000 (source) and it contains the University of Chicago, which is highly likely to contain people who agree that AI poses a risk to humanity. Per IIWDIWDWMUS, if we assume that:10% of people who moved through a given location in that region saw my poster80% of people in that region of Chicago are AI doomers (per Politico poll, the base rate in America of voters thinking any AI risk exists is 78% with 63% thinking the risk is at least moderate. These numbers increase by 6% and 7% respectively for people who voted for Harris in 2024, we average between 84% and 70% then round up by 3% to adjust for estimated increase from being near the University of Chicago)And 5% of AI doomers who saw at least one poster signed up for the march (the number of people already signed up for the march is negligible)Then running the numbers, I will have created ~188 new attendants to the Don't Build It march in this month, and far smaller numbers in the following months as most people who would have attended would have already seen a poster. The number might be higher if my made-up statistics are wrong, if people get their families to sign up as well, or if there is some high rate of people 'passing through' (I conservatively assume that 5000 monthly foot traffic generally means the same 5000 people walking around rather than getting refreshed). items.title: It’s Not About The Money Until It Is. The Middleman.
items.content: The Necessary MiddlemanMoney has no inherent value by itself; it’s a social construct. Its value comes from the things you buy with it. Why did we create money? For fluidity in trading; if I want to buy a table and the seller wants an air conditioner, I’d have to find someone who has one. But if they want something for the air conditioner that I don’t have, I’d be sent on another wild goose chase. With money, there’s no need to be sent on a wild goose chase; I give money for the table and the seller uses that money to buy themselves an air conditioner. We all have heard the saying, “Cut out the middleman,” and that’s true if the middleman is unnecessary and makes things more expensive and complicated than they need to be. But in some cases, the middleman is needed to make things more efficient.First Book is the largest literacy non-profit in the nation and made over $92 in revenue with $16.5 million for their services in the fiscal year of 2024. First Book is also a social enterprise and could be compared to a startup, but rather than provide a product, they provide a service by providing teachers with books at steeply discounted rates. The publishing industry is notoriously difficult to predict demand. If a book becomes in high demand, publishers can order a book to be printed in extreme bulk, which drastically lowers the unit price. If demand meets supply, they make stronger profits per unit. If demand is not as high as projected, they lose money on the books printed. First Book overcomes this by leveraging its network of 600,000 teachers to determine which books are in high demand. They then order those books in extreme bulk, allowing them to sell to teachers for steeply discounted prices while still making substantial profits even though their profit margins per unit are quite low. items.title: Reflections on 37 weeks of hosting EA/LW/ACX board games
items.content: (Epistemic Status: Personal experience, supplemented with good, though slightly flawed, data)At the start of 2025, I moved across the country to a city (Boston) I knew little about and that was filled entirely with people I didn’t know. Nearly two years later, I’m now happier, more satisfied, and have a better social life than ever before, and it is basically all downstream of deciding, at the start of 2026, that I was going to start hosting board games. After successfully hosting an initial board game night and querying attendees on continued interest, I committed myself to hosting every week until people lost interest or I was otherwise prevented from continuing. More than 9 months later, I am very happy to say that I am still hosting (approximately) every week (I’ve hosted ~37 out of the 45 weeks).In terms of specific life-improvements, I think that hosting board games has been directly and obviously causal in meeting my amazing girlfriend, turning several casual acquaintances into best friends, and generally increasing my average happiness by ~2-3 points (on a 10-point scale). I also just know a lot more people in the area, feel like I’m part of a community, and get to attend a lot more engaging and novel events with people I find interesting.These are the Partiful RSVP responses for individual board game nights so far.
